item.text: {"text":"The closest direct GRU precedent is [MTAM (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598): temporal gates modify information filtering and recurrent state transitions, with a time-aware GRU capturing short-term intent alongside historical memory. More recent work supports adaptive temporal modeling: [CussCtpm (IJCAI 2024)](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0255) combines GRUs and neural ODEs to represent continuously evolving POI preferences; [SAPM (2025)](https://cis.temple.edu/~jiewu/research/publications/Publication_files/2025-TWeb-Stability-aware%20Preference%20Modeling%20for%20Sequential%20Recommendation.pdf) uses multi-head GRUs and stability-conditioned fusion of long- and short-term interests. [Long-Term Interest Clock (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15817) retrieves relevant older behaviors and applies time-gap-aware attention, suggesting that temporal relevance need not decrease uniformly with age. These are architectural precedents, not evidence of gains under the pinned Amazon evaluation.\n\nA compatible experimental hypothesis is one jointly trained GRU whose reset/update gates receive normalized log inter-event gaps, optionally with learned per-dimension retention rates so durable interests can survive longer than transient intent. This is a proposed adaptation, not an established result from the cited studies. First verify padding invariance: identical valid histories with different amounts of left padding should produce identical states and scores; padding must neither update hidden state nor advance elapsed time, and readout must select the final nonpadding position. Only then compare ordinary GRU, fixed decay, and learned retention using the same histories, seeds, training budget, and macro validation HR@10. Existing confounded context-removal measurements cannot establish that older history is harmful. Use observed historical timestamps only; do not assume the next interaction time is available at inference."}
